title: Which Word Carries the Water
logline: Farmers gather under a tree to decide how the tank's water will be shared for the coming season. Elders argue for how it has always been done; younger farmers argue for their own standing and results. The harvest depends on which voice wins.
human_question: In an argument that matters, when does a person switch from arguing the facts to arguing their own standing?

premise.story: A real farmers' organisation meeting deciding water release for an ancient irrigation tank: speeches, interruptions, appeals to tradition, appeals to personal record and standing, and the decision that is finally reached.
premise.place: A meeting under a tree or in a village hall, served by a tank that has irrigated this land for generations.
premise.experience: The viewer sits in the meeting as the argument moves, without anyone quite noticing, between what is true and who is owed respect, and feels how much a season's harvest rides on the outcome.

concept_links.why: The sources distinguish two different ways of holding on that never occupy a mind at the same moment: fixed wrong view, insisting 'this is how things are', and conceit, insisting on one's own rank, 'this is how I stand' [C022-P:L91–L113; C022-M:L27–L31]. A heated meeting about a shared resource is a real place to watch speakers move between these two different grips, without the film needing to name either.

Both sources agree these two never coincide in one moment, though they explain it differently: Pradeepika says conceit is as strong an unwholesome state as wrong view, so the mind cannot hold both at once; Margaya says they are simply different kinds of grasping, over what is true and over where one stands [C026-P:L35; C026-M:L17].

what_camera_could_observe: The meeting itself: seating, order of speaking, interruptions
Elders appealing to precedent and how things have always been done
Younger farmers appealing to their own results, effort or standing
The moment the argument turns personal, and the moment it turns back to the water
The final decision, and the walk home
what_must_be_real: The meeting, the dispute and its outcome must be genuine and unscripted, with every participant's consent. Every side must be shown fairly and the film must not take a position on who was right.

possible_arc.opening: The tank at dawn, low or full depending on the season.
possible_arc.turn: The meeting grows heated, and voices shift between fact and standing.
possible_arc.ending_open: Whatever the farmers actually decide, and how they carry it afterwards, ends the film.

requirements: A village served by an ancient irrigation tank with an active farmers' organisation
A genuine water-allocation meeting occurring during the filming window
Consent from all participants, including those on both sides of the dispute

suggestions.name: A tank-irrigated farming village
suggestions.region: Anuradhapura or Polonnaruwa district, North Central Province
suggestions.why: The dry zone's ancient tank-irrigation system remains central to village farming life and organised water-sharing decisions in this region.
suggestions.season_notes: Tied to the seasonal water-release cycle ahead of cultivation.
suggestions.verify: A specific tank, village and meeting must be found and confirmed; this is a region-level suggestion only.

risks: Turning a real dispute over livelihoods into a simple morality play
Appearing to take a side in a genuine, ongoing community disagreement
Identifying individuals in ways that could affect real standing or relationships in the village
drop_if: No genuine water-allocation meeting occurs during the filming window
Participants are unwilling to have a real dispute filmed

connections.note: Both are set in dry-zone farmland where a real threat to a livelihood tests fear and anger together.
Two possible studies of status and possession; a slate might choose one over the other to avoid repetition.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed. Everything above is a research direction.
